title: More thoughts on American Psycho:@Joe Weinberg  #broadway #musicalthe...
transcript: Duncan Sheik was a more important musical theatre writer than I think most people even realize, and I'm devastated to hear of his tragic passing. Spring Awakening will be his lasting legacy in the musical theatre world, and rightly so. But I also want to take a moment to talk about some of his lesser known work and some of the ways in which he was quietly or not so quietly pushing the art form forward. at the time of recording, I've seen five of his musicals live on stage, but of course Spring Awakening was the first. It blew my mind when I saw it on tour in 2008, when I saw the Deaf West revival in 2015, when I saw the reunion concert in 2021, and even on recent relistens, it struck me just how well his work on it has held up. It still feels so fresh and vibrant and avant garde in its own way,, even 20 years later. Sheik and his collaborators were unafraid to use music in unconventional ways, making space for the abstract and the mood driven music that traditional Broadway gatekeepers will tell you is not the “right” way to make a musical. But he understood that an equally valid way of telling stories through music was to work on the audience on a deeper, primal level, evoking a feeling that does inform their experience of the story and the character journeys, even if they're not totally aware of it a lot of the same can be said about the American Psycho musical, which I did a whole video about that I'll link in the caption about how I think this show was ahead of its time with a sense of tone and style that defied traditional musical theatre norms and managed to be funny and hypnotic at the same time. Another common thread here is how he used genre. And, you know, he was certainly not the first person to incorporate pop, rock and folk into musical theatre, but I think he carried the torch into the 21st century at a time when fewer people were doing it and even fewer were doing it well. Sheik was famously a songwriter in his own right, outside of musical theatre, and I think that afforded him a sense of vision and perspective that we don't always see. And not to get on my soapbox too much, but I do believe that being in conversation with outside genre is the main way of keeping musical theatre alive and relevant. The next one I saw from him was Alice by heart, which was unfortunately one of the most embarrassing trainwrecks I've ever seen in musical theatre. But even then, Sheik’s work on it was the one saving grace. He did the score for The Secret Life of bees musical, which was in some ways more traditional in terms of how it incorporated music into the story. But he was working at an extremely high level of craft and intelligence on this one. I would argue it's maybe his most technically well-written composition work for musical theatre. And it's also just haunting and exhilarating. And it's ludicrous that we don't have a cast album for this one. But the last one I saw from him was a little known off Broadway musical that I think only I liked. It was an adaptation of the movie Bob and Carol and Ted and Alice about a pair of swinger couples. And again, he was experimenting with tone and structure. It was quiet and subdued, but also had this strange, quirky humor. The songs were deliberately very short and broken up with a lot of dialogue, giving us these unpredictable flashes of intimate introspection for the characters. And again, we were playing with genre. There were elements of, like, soft rock and jazz to evoke the intimate late sixties feel. I'm glad that Sheik's legacy will live on through revivals, through musicals that are still upcoming, like memoirs of an Amorous Gentleman. But I both fear and celebrate that there may never be another musical theatre writer quite like him again.
